```text
Digital Twin View
```

---

# 126. Facility Explorer

Shows:

```text
labs
machines
capabilities
availability
locations
```

---

# 127. Equipment Detail

Shows:

```text
capabilities
constraints
calendar
maintenance
calibration
projects using it
```

---

# 128. Capacity View

Shows:

```text
available hours
reserved hours
queues
bottlenecks
```

---

# 129. Manufacturing Resolver

For a Project:

```text
required physical operations
candidate providers
cost
lead time
constraints
```

---

# 130. Digital Twin View

Shows:

```text
current state
recent events
telemetry summary
active tasks
maintenance state
```

---

# 131. Physical API

Minimum:

```text
GET /facilities
GET /equipment
GET /equipment/{id}/availability
POST /physical/resolve
POST /reservations
GET /capacity
POST /simulation/run
```

---

# 132. Reservation approval

Booking expensive/shared resource may require:

```text
Decision
```

before reservation becomes active.

---

# 133. Physical Resource Lock

Analog of project.lock:

```yaml
bindings:
  environmental_test:
    provider: lab_4
    equipment: chamber_2
    slot: ...
```

---

# 134. Physical Execution Lock

Before starting test:

```text
sample
procedure
equipment
operator
time slot
```

must all be pinned.

---

# 135. Experiment reproducibility

A physical experiment should be reproducible from:

```text
procedure version
equipment
calibration
sample
software
environment
```

This can all be represented in World State.

---

# 136. Research + Physical integration

Now Research Observatory can move from:

```text
Paper
```

to:

```text
real experiment
```

without leaving the same architecture.

---

# 137. Funding + Physical integration

Funding call can fund:

```text
equipment
facility
pilot line
```

World State already knows:

```text
which physical bottleneck blocks which projects
```

So funding search becomes strategic.

---

# 138. GitHub + Physical integration

Software repo may control:

```text
robot
sensor
machine
```

Now repository capability and physical capability connect.

---

# 139. HN + Physical integration

Talent demand can include:

```text
robotics
manufacturing
lab operations
```

and Candidate capabilities can match Physical Projects.

---

# 140. Full Capability Supply Graph

Now providers include:

```text
Human
Team
AI Agent
Software
Repository
Service
Research Method
Lab
Equipment
Manufacturer
Funding Resource
```

This is essentially the complete resource model originally envisioned for the virtual technopark.

---

# 141. Full Gap Taxonomy

Now gap can be:

```text
Talent Gap
Technology Gap
Knowledge Gap
Data Gap
Funding Gap
Lab Gap
Equipment Gap
Material Gap
Manufacturing Gap
Logistics Gap
Governance Gap
```

But semantically they are all:

```text
Requirement not yet satisfied
```

That is one of the strongest architectural simplifications in the whole design.

---

# 142. Universal Resolution Loop

```text
Requirement
↓
Is it satisfied?
   │
   ├── YES → continue
   │
   ├── UNKNOWN → gather evidence
   │
   └── NO → create Gap
                 ↓
            search providers
                 ↓
            resolution options
                 ↓
            validate
                 ↓
            decision
                 ↓
             binding
```

This same loop works for almost every resource class.

---

# 143. Physical World + MMORPG Interface

Now the 3D layer can finally become genuinely useful.

Not merely:

```text
a decorative virtual city
```

but:

```text
live representation of:
facilities
machines
robots
projects
goods
queues
```

---

# 144. Strategic level

Zoomed out:

```text
city / technopark
```

shows:

```text
labs
organizations
programs
resource flows
```

---

# 145. Operational level

Zoom in:

```text
factory
```

shows:

```text
machines
work cells
queues
robots
```

---

# 146. Equipment level

Zoom further:

```text
machine state
current job
maintenance
```

---

# 147. Same entity IDs at all levels

Crucially:

```text
Machine #42
```

in 3D is the same entity as:

```text
resource_42
```

in PostgreSQL.

No duplicate game-world database.

---

# 148. Game mechanics become operations

For example:

```text
drag Job to Machine
```

UI generates:

```text
ASSIGN Action
```

Runtime checks:

```text
capability
capacity
safety
booking
```

Then executes or rejects.

---

# 149. Missions become Projects

A "mission":

```text
Build tactile sensor prototype
```

is actual Project IR.

Progress bars derive from real Actions.

---

# 150. Tech tree becomes dependency graph

Unlocked technology:

```text
not arbitrary XP
```

but:

```text
validated capability
```

---

# 151. Resources become actual resources

```text
machine time
lab access
compute
materials
funding
people
```

The game-like world therefore becomes a **serious operational interface** rather than only gamification.

---

# 152. Next architectural transition

After this module, all major resource classes are represented:

```text
People
AI
Code
Knowledge
Funding
Physical infrastructure
```

The next logical layer is no longer another Observatory.

It is:

# **Universal Capability Market & Resource Exchange v0.1**

Not necessarily a monetary marketplace.

Rather a unified system where:

```text
Projects publish Capability Demand
Resources publish Capability Supply
```

and the system continuously resolves:

```text
Demand ↔ Supply
```

across:

```text
humans
AI
software
labs
equipment
organizations
funding
```

---

# 153. Universal Capability Market

Core abstraction:

```text
DEMAND SIDE

Project / Task / Program
REQUIRES
Capability
```

versus:

```text
SUPPLY SIDE

Resource
PROVIDES
Capability
```

The matcher no longer cares initially whether the provider is a human, repo, lab, or AI agent.

It first reasons in capability space.

---

# 154. Then provider-specific constraints apply

For Person:

```text
availability
location
employment
```

For Software:

```text
license
integration
```

For Equipment:

```text
capacity
location
booking
```

For Funding:

```text
eligibility
deadline
```

Thus one universal marketplace can have specialized resolvers.

---

# 155. Why this is important

It finally converts all previous Observatories into a single live economic/technical coordination layer:

```text
OBSERVATORIES
↓
WORLD STATE
↓
CAPABILITY SUPPLY / DEMAND
↓
RESOURCE EXCHANGE
↓
PROJECT ASSEMBLY
↓
EXECUTION
```

---

# 156. Final result of this stage

At this point, the virtual technopark has a complete skeleton:

```text
observe the world
↓
understand capabilities
↓
find gaps
↓
find resources
↓
assemble projects
↓
fund them
↓
allocate physical infrastructure
↓
execute
↓
measure
↓
update world
```

That means the next module — **Universal Capability Market & Resource Exchange** — can unify everything developed so far into one continuous coordination mechanism rather than a collection of separate Observatories.
contents.title: Physical Infrastructure, Labs, Equipment & Manufacturing Observatory v0.1

contents.content: Дальше логично формализовать именно **Universal Capability Market & Resource Exchange**: как выглядят заявки спроса и предложения, как работает непрерывное matching между проектами и ресурсами, как учитывать время, стоимость, доступность, приоритеты, составные решения и как из этого постепенно получается настоящий внутренний рынок/биржа возможностей виртуального технопарка.
Продолжение

# Universal Capability Market & Resource Exchange v0.1

## 1. Главный переход

До этого система уже умеет:

```text
наблюдать мир
↓
извлекать capabilities
↓
видеть gaps
↓
находить resources
↓
собирать project configurations
```

Теперь нужен слой, который делает это **не эпизодически по запросу**, а постоянно.

То есть:

```text
Projects continuously publish Demand
Resources continuously publish Supply
↓
Capability Market
↓
matching / allocation / reallocation
```

Это уже не обычный marketplace.

Это **рынок возможностей и дефицитов**.

---

# 2. Capability Market ≠ рынок вакансий

Обычный job market:

```text
Employer
↔
Person
```

Здесь:

```text
Project / Task / Program
↔
Capability
↔
Resource
```

А Resource может быть:

```text
Person
Team
AI Agent
Software
Repository
Service
Research Method
Dataset
Lab
Equipment
Organization
Funding
```

Поэтому рынок становится универсальным.

---

# 3. Fundamental abstraction

Спрос:

```text
DEMAND:
Entity REQUIRES Capability
```

Предложение:

```text
SUPPLY:
Resource PROVIDES Capability
```

Matching:

```text
REQUIREMENT
↔
PROVIDER
```

Это центральная формула всей системы.

---

# 4. Demand Order

Можно ввести application-level объект:

```yaml
demand_order:
  id: demand_001
  requester: project_17
  capability: secure_agent_execution

  target_depth: production

  quantity: 1

  constraints:
    - remote_allowed
    - self_hosted_required

  needed_by: 2026-11-01

  status: OPEN
```

Это не новый IIR Core type.

Он компилируется в:

```text
Project REQUIRES Capability
+
Constraints
+
Temporal Context
```

---

# 5. Supply Offer

Аналогично:

```yaml
supply_offer:
  id: supply_001

  provider: resource_44
  capability: secure_agent_execution

  depth: production

  availability:
    from: ...
    capacity: ...

  conditions:
    ...
```

В IIR:

```text
Resource PROVIDES Capability
+
Availability Claims
+
Constraints
```

---

# 6. Почему нужны Orders/Offers как application objects

Хотя semantic truth уже хранится в Claims, exchange layer должен видеть:

```text
кто сейчас ищет
кто сейчас предлагает
в каком объёме
на какой срок
```

То есть:

```text
Capability Registry
```

говорит:

> Кто вообще умеет?

А:

```text
Capability Market
```

говорит:

> Кто сейчас доступен и кому это сейчас нужно?

---

# 7. Market State

Минимально:

```text
Open Demand
Open Supply
Potential Matches
Committed Bindings
Waitlists
Expired Offers
```

---

# 8. Demand status

Freeze application enum:

```text
DRAFT
OPEN
MATCHING
NEGOTIATING
BOUND
PARTIALLY_FILLED
FULFILLED
CANCELLED
EXPIRED
```

---

# 9. Supply status

```text
AVAILABLE
PARTIALLY_ALLOCATED
ALLOCATED
UNAVAILABLE
EXPIRED
```

---

# 10. Capacity matters

Один Resource может предоставить capability нескольким projects.

Например:

```text
Person A:
20 h/week
```

или:

```text
GPU cluster:
500 GPU-hours/week
```

или:

```text
Lab:
2 experiment slots/day
```

Поэтому supply:

```text
capability
+
capacity
+
time
```

---

# 11. Time-dependent Market

Вместо статического:

```text
Resource available = YES
```

нужно:

```text
Resource available
from t1 to t2
with capacity C
```

---

# 12. Capacity Reservation

После tentative match:

```text
reserve
```

часть capacity.

Например:

```text
Person A:
20 h/week

Project X:
reserve 8

remaining:
12
```

---

# 13. Reservation ≠ final assignment

Полезно иметь:

```text
PROPOSED
HELD
CONFIRMED
RELEASED
```

Это уменьшает race conditions.

---

# 14. Market Event

Например:

```text
DEMAND_OPENED
SUPPLY_OPENED
MATCH_PROPOSED
CAPACITY_RESERVED
BINDING_CONFIRMED
BINDING_RELEASED
DEMAND_FULFILLED
```

Все остаются Events.

---

# 15. Capability Unit

Не вся capability измеряется одинаково.

Например:

```text
security review
```

может быть:

```text
1 review
```

Но:

```text
software engineering
```

может быть:

```text
hours/week
```

А:

```text
GPU inference
```

может быть:

```text
GPU-hours
```

Поэтому capability offer должен поддерживать:

```text
unit
```

---

# 16. Fungible vs Non-Fungible Capability

Некоторые resources почти взаимозаменяемы:

```text
100 GPU-hours
```

Другие нет:

```text
specific expert
specific microscope
specific proprietary dataset
```

Это важное различие.

---

# 17. Fungibility

Можно хранить:

```text
HIGH
MEDIUM
LOW
```

на уровне market semantics.

Например:

```text
cloud compute = high
senior domain expert = low
```

---

# 18. Matching stages

Universal Market лучше разделить на пять этапов:

```text
1. Retrieval
2. Feasibility
3. Compatibility
4. Composition
5. Commitment
```

---

# 19. Retrieval

Найти:

```text
all plausible providers
```

по capability:

```text
exact
alias
taxonomy
semantic similarity
```

---

# 20. Feasibility

Проверить HARD constraints:

```text
availability
location
license
capacity
eligibility
deadline
```

---

# 21. Compatibility

Проверить:

```text
depth
context
integration effort
quality evidence
work style
technology fit
```

---

# 22. Composition

Если один provider недостаточен:

```text
compose multiple resources
```

---

# 23. Commitment

После:

```text
human / organization / policy approval
```

создаётся Binding.

---

# 24. Binding

```yaml
binding:
  demand_id: demand_001
  provider_id: resource_44

  quantity: 8
  unit: hour/week

  valid_from: ...
  valid_to: ...

  state: CONFIRMED
```

---

# 25. Binding as project.lock component

То есть:

```text
project.lock
```

может быть набором confirmed capability bindings.

---

# 26. Market Resolver

Pipeline:

```text
Demand
↓
Candidate Providers
↓
Hard Filters
↓
Evidence
↓
Capacity Check
↓
Composite Alternatives
↓
Binding Proposal
```

---

# 27. Supply fragmentation

Например Project требует:

```text
40 h/week backend engineering
```

Но market has:

```text
Person A: 20
Person B: 10
AI Agent C: equivalent bounded contribution
```

System may build composite supply.

---

# 28. But capacity is not always additive

Two junior engineers:

```text
10h + 10h
```

не всегда equivalent to:

```text
20h senior expertise
```

Поэтому composition must respect:

```text
capability depth
coordination cost
role structure
```

---

# 29. Complementarity

Некоторые resources усиливают друг друга.

Например:

```text
AI coding agent
+
senior reviewer
```

может outperform each alone for certain tasks.

То есть market should support:

```text
COMPLEMENTARY resources
```

---

# 30. Substitutability vs Complementarity

Graph relations:

```text
ALTERNATIVE_TO
COMPLEMENTS
REQUIRES_TOGETHER
```

можно держать в library ontology.

---

# 31. Bundle Offer

Можно создать:

```text
bundle:
  person_A
  repo_B
  AI_agent_C
```

provides:

```text
secure_browser_runtime
```

Это derived composite Resource.

---

# 32. Team as Composite Resource

`TEAM` уже есть как Resource.

Он может иметь:

```text
member resources
aggregate capabilities
```

---

# 33. Dynamic Team

Market может создать:

```text
temporary Team Hypothesis
```

для одного project.

После approval:

```text
Team Resource
```

становится committed.

---

# 34. Market does not need money

Очень важно.

Exchange can optimize:

```text
capability allocation
```

без financial price.

Например внутри university or technopark:

```text
machine time
expert hours
lab slots
```

can be allocated by priority, quota or policy.

---

# 35. Allocation Modes

Useful application enum:

```text
MARKET_PRICE
FIXED_PRICE
INTERNAL_QUOTA
PRIORITY_ALLOCATION
GRANT_FUNDED
BARTER
VOLUNTEER
SHARED_POOL
```

---

# 36. Internal Technopark Market

Пример:

```text
10 projects
3 security experts
2 labs
limited compute
```

Market resolves:

```text
who gets what when
```

---

# 37. Priority constraints

Project can have:

```text
critical
normal
exploratory
```

But system should not use priority as universal human-worth score.

Это только resource allocation priority.

---

# 38. Scarcity

Capability scarcity can be derived from:

```text
demand
supply
availability
substitutability
```

---

# 39. Scarcity ≠ value

Редкая capability:

```text
not necessarily important
```

and important capability:

```text
not necessarily rare
```

Need separate dimensions.

---

# 40. Scarcity Vector

```text
Demand volume
Available supply
Time-to-capability
Substitution options
Geographic constraints
Depth requirements
```

---

# 41. Market Signal

Example:

```text
agent security
```

may show:

```text
high demand
low supply
few substitutes
```

This becomes:

```text
Capability Shortage Signal
```

---

# 42. Shortage can trigger interventions

Not only:

```text
raise price
```

but:

```text
TRAIN
AUTOMATE
BUILD TOOL
STANDARDIZE
CREATE SHARED TEAM
```

This is a major difference from ordinary markets.

---

# 43. Market as intervention engine

Traditional market:

```text
scarcity → price
```

Innovation OS:

```text
scarcity
→ diagnose cause
→ create new capability supply
```

---

# 44. Training Opportunity

Example:

```text
20 projects need capability X
2 experts available
```

Opportunity Engine may create:

```text
Training Program
```

---

# 45. Tooling Opportunity

If shortage is because work is repetitive:

```text
automation project
```

may create new supply.

---

# 46. Shared Service Opportunity

Example:

```text
security reviews repeated
```

Create:

```text
Shared Security Office
```

as Resource.

---

# 47. Standardization Opportunity

If every project needs custom adapters:

```text
common interface
```

may increase supply efficiency.

---

# 48. Market creates its own supply

This is important.

The system is not only allocating fixed resources.

It can generate projects that increase future supply.

---

# 49. Supply Creation Loop

```text
Scarcity
↓
Opportunity
↓
Project
↓
New Resource / Capability
↓
Supply increases
```

---

# 50. Demand Creation Loop

New capability may also create new demand:

```text
New technology
↓
new feasible projects
↓
new capability demand
```

So market is dynamic.

---

# 51. Capability Price

If financial market enabled, one can track:

```text
hourly rate
license cost
service cost
machine-hour
```

But avoid universal normalization.

---

# 52. Capability Cost

Better concept:

```text
Cost to obtain capability
```

rather than:

```text
price of capability
```

because acquisition may include:

```text
integration
training
maintenance
review
```

---

# 53. TCC inside Market

For each option:

```text
TCC
TTC
risk
control
```

already developed earlier.

Market uses them continuously.

---

# 54. Opportunity Cost

Allocating Resource A to Project X means it may be unavailable to Y.

This introduces:

```text
opportunity cost
```

at portfolio level.

---

# 55. Example

One security expert can support:

```text
Project A
or
Projects B+C
```

Portfolio optimizer can expose alternatives.

---

# 56. Do not auto-optimize everything

Human strategy remains above market.

Market can show:

```text
allocation scenarios
```

not silently choose strategic priorities.

---

# 57. Market + Portfolio Intelligence

Architecture:

```text
Portfolio priorities
↓
Allocation policies
↓
Capability Market
↓
Bindings
```

---

# 58. Market + Runtime

Runtime consumes confirmed bindings:

```text
Task READY
↓
binding available
↓
execute
```

---

# 59. Market + Event Bus

When:

```text
RESOURCE_UNAVAILABLE
```

market receives event.

Affected bindings:

```text
DEGRADED
```

Demand reopens.

---

# 60. Continuous Reallocation

Example:

```text
Person A unavailable
↓
3 tasks lose provider
↓
market finds substitutes
↓
proposes rebinding
```

---

# 61. Hot Standby

Critical capability may have:

```text
primary provider
backup provider
```

Binding model should support both.

---

# 62. Redundant Supply

For critical project:

```text
security approval
```

can require:

```text
2 independent reviewers
```

This is deliberate redundancy.

---

# 63. Reliability-Aware Market

Provider has capability-specific operational metrics:

```text
availability
completion rate
latency
verification pass rate
```

for AI/tools/services.

---

# 64. Human performance caution

For people, avoid reductive global rankings.

Use task-specific evidence:

```text
public work
documented experience
explicit availability
```

rather than hidden universal worker scores.

---

# 65. Resource Reputation should be contextual

For Software:

```text
maintenance history
```

For Lab:

```text
calibration / turnaround
```

For AI Agent:

```text
verification pass rate
```

Different resource classes need different evidence.

---

# 66. Market Explainability

Every match should answer:

```text
Why was this provider retrieved?
Why is it feasible?
What is unknown?
What blocks it?
Why is composition needed?
```

---

# 67. No black-box 92%

The UI should show:

```text
coverage
constraints
evidence
capacity
cost
time
unknowns
```

---

# 68. Market Query

Example:

```text
Find operational providers for:
secure_browser_execution

needed:
within 4 weeks

constraints:
self-hosted
EU-compatible
```

---

# 69. Query result

```text
Option A:
Repo + internal engineer

Option B:
Commercial service

Option C:
External specialist + OSS

Option D:
Build internally
```

---

# 70. Bidirectional Market

Not only:

```text
Demand → Supply
```

also:

```text
Supply → Demand
```

Example:

```text
new GPU cluster available
```

System asks:

```text
which blocked projects can now use it?
```

---

# 71. New Talent Event

```text
new specialist discovered
```

→ scan relevant gaps.

---

# 72. New Repo Event

```text
new repo discovered
```

→ scan technology gaps.

---

# 73. New Grant Event

```text
new funding resource
```

→ scan funding gaps.

---

# 74. New Lab Event

```text
new facility capacity
```

→ scan physical gaps.

---

# 75. Universal Reverse Index

Need:

```text
Capability → Open Demand
Capability → Available Supply
```

This is central index.

---

# 76. Demand Graph

```text
Capability
↓
Projects requiring it
↓
Tasks requiring it
```

---

# 77. Supply Graph

```text
Capability
↓
Resources providing it
↓
capacity / evidence / constraints
```

---

# 78. Market Snapshot

At any time:

```text
Capability X

Demand:
14 projects

Supply:
5 resources

Committed:
3

Available:
2

Unknown:
4 possible resources
```

---

# 79. Market Forecast

Using planned projects:

```text
future demand
```

can be estimated.

But label as:

```text
planned/forecast demand
```

not current demand.

---

# 80. Forward Capacity Planning

Example:

```text
next quarter:
3 projects will require photonics testing
```

System can warn:

```text
lab capacity insufficient
```

before projects block.

---

# 81. Pre-booking

Physical resources can be reserved ahead.

But reservation policy must avoid:

```text
capacity hoarding
```

---

# 82. Reservation Policy

Could use:

```text
expiry
deposit
priority
maximum hold time
```

depending on domain.

---

# 83. Market Deadlock

Possible situation:

```text
Project A waits Resource B
Project B waits Resource A
```

or resource dependency cycle.

Need:

```text
deadlock detector
```

---

# 84. Capability Dependency Deadlock

Example:

```text
Lab requires certified operator
Operator training requires lab access
```

Potential cycle.

System should detect and suggest bridge.

---

# 85. Bridge Resource

Temporary:

```text
external service
```

can break deadlock.

---

# 86. Market Liquidity

Interesting concept.

A capability is liquid if:

```text
many interchangeable providers
quick acquisition
low switching cost
```

---

# 87. Illiquid Capability

Example:

```text
rare scientific instrument
specific legal authority
unique domain expert
```

---

# 88. Liquidity matters for risk

Projects depending on illiquid capabilities need:

```text
earlier planning
redundancy
```

---

# 89. Capability Liquidity Vector

```text
provider count
substitutability
time-to-acquire
switching cost
geographic restrictions
```

---

# 90. Bottleneck Market

Capabilities with:

```text
high demand
low liquidity
high strategic importance
```

become candidates for strategic investment.

---

# 91. Capability Development Market

Could publish:

```text
Demand:
need capability X
```

and allow providers to respond:

```text
we can develop it
```

So supply need not already exist.

---

# 92. Build Offer

Example:

```text
Organization A:
can build custom sensor in 8 weeks
```

This is:

```text
future supply
```

conditional on project.

---

# 93. Conditional Supply

Supply can be:

```text
AVAILABLE_NOW
BUILD_TO_ORDER
TRAINABLE
RESEARCH_REQUIRED
```

---

# 94. Market therefore spans current and potential supply

```text
Current Supply
Potential Supply
Frontier Supply
```

---

# 95. Capability Maturity Dimension

Potential provider may offer:

```text
PROTOTYPE
```

while project requires:

```text
PRODUCTION
```

This creates:

```text
maturity gap
```

not total absence.

---

# 96. Upgrade Path

System can propose:

```text
prototype provider
+
hardening project
```

instead of rejecting completely.

---

# 97. Capability Upgrade Contract

Example:

```text
Current:
WORKING

Target:
PRODUCTION

Needed:
tests
security
documentation
operations
```

This itself becomes Project.

---

# 98. Market + Project Generator

Gap can resolve in two ways:

```text
find existing supply
```

or:

```text
create project to produce supply
```

This is extremely important.

---

# 99. Make-or-Match decision

```text
MATCH:
existing provider

MAKE:
create new provider/capability
```

The system compares both.

---

# 100. Example

Need:

```text
robot tactile dataset
```

No dataset exists.

Options:

```text
buy dataset
partner
generate dataset
simulate dataset
```

If no provider:

```text
Dataset Creation Project
```

---

# 101. Resource Exchange Interface

For human user:

```text
Open Demands
Available Supply
Suggested Matches
Composite Solutions
Unresolved Gaps
```

---

# 102. Demand Detail

Shows:

```text
requester
capability
depth
deadline
constraints
current coverage
candidate providers
```

---

# 103. Supply Detail

Shows:

```text
resource
capabilities
capacity
availability
conditions
open demand matches
```

---

# 104. Market Map

2D graph:

```text
Demand nodes
↔
Capability nodes
↔
Supply nodes
```

Coloring can indicate state, but UI detail is later.

---

# 105. 3D market metaphor

In MMORPG-like interface:

```text
Projects = demand hubs
Resources = active units
Capabilities = routes/ports
```

But actual matching still happens in semantic graph.

---

# 106. Capability Exchange as internal operating system

This layer begins to resemble:

```text
scheduler + market + ERP + matching engine
```

for heterogeneous resources.

---

# 107. Market Clearing

In simple case:

```text
many demands
many supplies
limited capacity
```

we need allocation algorithm.

---

# 108. Allocation Problem

Inputs:

```text
Demand_i
Supply_j
Compatibility_ij
Capacity_j
Constraints
Priorities
```

Output:

```text
Bindings
Unfilled Demand
Unused Capacity
```

---

# 109. MVP algorithm

Do not start with complex auction theory.

First:

```text
hard filter
↓
weighted bipartite matching
↓
capacity constraints
```

or greedy allocation.

---

# 110. Later optimization

Could use:

```text
linear programming
mixed integer programming
min-cost flow
constraint programming
```

depending on case.

---

# 111. Market Clearing Objective

Do not define one universal objective.

Possible scenarios:

```text
maximize critical capability coverage
minimize unmet MUST requirements
minimize cost
minimize delay
maximize resilience
```

Human/policy selects scenario.

---

# 112. Multi-objective allocation

Results can be Pareto configurations.

Example:

```text
Scenario A:
fastest

Scenario B:
lowest cost

Scenario C:
highest resilience
```

---

# 113. Auctions optional, not foundational

For external open marketplace, auction mechanisms may later be useful.

But internal technopark does not need auctions initially.

---

# 114. Negotiation

Some supply requires:

```text
rate negotiation
scope negotiation
availability negotiation
```

This is separate from matching.

---

# 115. Negotiation State

```text
MATCHED
CONTACT_PENDING
NEGOTIATING
AGREED
DECLINED
```

---

# 116. No automatic outreach by default

System can identify match.

External communication remains separate approved Action.

This continues the same boundary used for HN.

---

# 117. Contract Generation

After agreement:

```text
binding
```

may require legal/administrative Artifact:

```text
employment contract
service agreement
lab booking
grant agreement
```

---

# 118. Contract as operational binding evidence

Project lock can reference:

```text
Decision
+
Contract Artifact
```

for confirmed provider.

---

# 119. Resource Exchange and ERP

Once binding exists:

```text
resource
budget
time
tasks
```

flow into execution.

This is why Capability Market can become the central planning layer of an ERP-like system.

---

# 120. Traditional ERP vs Capability ERP

Traditional ERP often asks:

```text
what inventory / employee / order exists?
```

Capability ERP asks:

```text
what can this organization actually do right now?
what is missing?
what can be assembled?
```

This is more semantic.

---

# 121. Organization Capability Balance Sheet

Interesting output:

```text
Internal Capabilities
External Capabilities
Available Capacity
Committed Capacity
Strategic Gaps
```

---

# 122. Capability Balance Sheet example

```text
Agent evaluation:
internal 40 h/week
external 20 h/week
demand 70 h/week
gap 10

Security:
internal 5
external 30
demand 15
surplus external options
```

---

# 123. Capability Liability

A project dependency on one fragile provider can be treated as:

```text
capability liability
```

not financial liability, but operational exposure.

---

# 124. Capability Asset

A reusable:

```text
tool
dataset
trained team
shared lab
```

that serves many projects is a strategic capability asset.

---

# 125. Investment logic

Portfolio Intelligence can ask:

```text
Which capability asset would resolve the largest recurring gaps?
```

This connects Market directly to Strategic Bottleneck Engine.

---

# 126. Resource Exchange → Program creation

Repeated demand:

```text
many projects request X
```

and no adequate supply:

```text
Program:
Develop Capability X
```

---

# 127. Resource Exchange → Organization design

Repeated demand for:

```text
security
grant management
AI evaluation
```

can justify permanent teams.

So org structure becomes data-driven.

---

# 128. Dynamic Organization Compiler

Potential future module:

```text
Demand Graph
↓
stable repeated clusters
↓
suggest organizational units
```

---

# 129. Example

If:

```text
20 projects repeatedly need:
security review
threat modeling
compliance
```

system may propose:

```text
Security Office
```

instead of project-by-project hiring.

---

# 130. Capability Market → Training Market

People can declare:

```text
WANTS_TO_LEARN
capability X
```

Projects declare:

```text
need capability X
```

Training programs bridge.

---

# 131. Apprenticeship Model

Example:

```text
Expert A
+
Learner B
+
Project X
```

can create capability growth while delivering work.

---

# 132. Human Development Layer

Market should not only allocate existing human capabilities.

It can support:

```text
learning
mentorship
skill formation
```

This is more sustainable than pure competition for scarce specialists.

---

# 133. AI as Capability Multiplier

AI may increase effective capacity of people.

Example:

```text
one analyst
+
AI research agent
```

may cover more research tasks.

But multiplier must be empirical, task-specific.

---

# 134. Augmented Resource

Could represent:

```text
Human A + AI Tool B
```

as composite Resource.

---

# 135. Human-AI Bundle

Capability claims should be attached to:

```text
bundle configuration
```

not automatically to Human A alone.

---

# 136. Example

Human alone:

```text
10 reports/week
```

Human + AI:

```text
25 reports/week
```

if verified.

This creates operational evidence.

---

# 137. Market Experimentation

Low-risk tasks can test alternative resource configurations.

Example:

```text
Human only
vs
Human + AI
```

Measure:

```text
quality
time
cost
```

---

# 138. Capability productivity

Again, avoid universal worker productivity score.

Measure:

```text
specific task type
specific configuration
specific context
```

---

# 139. Resource Exchange API

Minimum:

```text
POST /market/demand
POST /market/supply

GET /market/demand
GET /market/supply

POST /market/match
POST /market/reserve
POST /market/bind
POST /market/release

GET /market/capabilities/{id}
```

---

# 140. Matching endpoint

Input:

```yaml
demand:
  capability: cap_x
  depth: production
  needed_by: ...
  constraints: ...
```

Output:

```text
individual providers
composite configurations
unknowns
blockers
```

---

# 141. Reverse endpoint

```text
GET /resources/{id}/market-opportunities
```

shows open demand relevant to Resource.

---

# 142. Event subscriptions

A Resource can subscribe:

```text
notify when matching demand appears
```

A Project:

```text
notify when new supply appears
```

---

# 143. Automation

This creates powerful condition watches:

```text
When capability X becomes available
→ reconsider project Y
```

---

# 144. Market Time Series

Over months:

```text
demand
supply
capacity
fill rate
TTC
```

per capability.

---

# 145. Capability Fill Rate

```text
fulfilled demand / total compatible demand
```

in defined population.

This helps identify persistent bottlenecks.

---

# 146. Time-to-Fill

For each demand:

```text
opened_at
→ fulfilled_at
```

Again domain-specific.

---

# 147. Market Learning

Store:

```text
which matches accepted
which rejected
why
which bindings succeeded
which failed
```

This is Gold Dataset for universal resolver.

---

# 148. Reason Codes

Examples:

```text
CAPABILITY_GAP
CAPACITY_INSUFFICIENT
LICENSE_BLOCK
LOCATION_BLOCK
COST_TOO_HIGH
TIMELINE_MISMATCH
WEAK_EVIDENCE
INTEGRATION_TOO_COMPLEX
```

---

# 149. Binding outcome

After execution:

```text
SUCCESS
PARTIAL
FAILED
CANCELLED
```

with reason.

This closes learning loop.

---

# 150. Market self-improvement

```text
Match
↓
Binding
↓
Outcome
↓
Error analysis
↓
Matcher improvement proposal
↓
Benchmark
↓
Approval
```

---

# 151. Universal Capability Market in overall architecture

```text
OBSERVATORIES
   │
   ├── HN
   ├── GitHub
   ├── Research
   ├── Funding
   └── Physical
        ↓
     WORLD STATE
        ↓
CAPABILITY SUPPLY / DEMAND
        ↓
UNIVERSAL CAPABILITY MARKET
        ↓
RESOURCE BINDINGS
        ↓
PROJECT / PROGRAM EXECUTION
        ↓
OUTCOMES
        ↓
WORLD STATE
```

---

# 152. Why this is a major architectural milestone

Previously we had:

```text
many specialized resolvers
```

Now they become adapters around a universal abstraction:

```text
Requirement ↔ Provider
```

This dramatically simplifies the whole Innovation OS.

---

# 153. Core equivalence

Employment:

```text
Project Gap ↔ Person
```

Software acquisition:

```text
Project Gap ↔ Repository
```

Research:

```text
Knowledge Gap ↔ Method/Researcher
```

Funding:

```text
Funding Gap ↔ Grant
```

Equipment:

```text
Physical Gap ↔ Lab
```

All are instances of the same market relation.

---

# 154. But providers remain heterogeneous

Universal abstraction does **not** mean pretending:

```text
person = machine = grant
```

It only means they all can satisfy requirements.

Each retains:

```text
its own state
constraints
ethics
permissions
cost model
```

---

# 155. Full loop

At this point the virtual technopark can operate as:

```text
Observe
↓
Model
↓
Publish Demand
↓
Discover Supply
↓
Compose
↓
Bind
↓
Execute
↓
Verify
↓
Learn
```

---

# 156. Next module

The next natural layer is:

# **Dynamic Organization & Program Formation Engine v0.1**

Because once the Capability Market continuously sees:

```text
repeated demand
repeated resource combinations
persistent shortages
stable collaboration clusters
```

it can begin asking:

```text
Which temporary teams should become permanent units?

Which repeated projects should become programs?

Which shared services should become departments?

Which recurring capability bundles define a new professional role?

Which organizations should collaborate repeatedly?
```

That module would turn the Capability Market from a matching system into a mechanism for **automatically discovering the organizational structure best suited to the actual flow of work**—while keeping final organizational decisions human-governed.
contents.title: Universal Capability Market & Resource Exchange v0.1

contents.content: Продолжение и на руском

Продолжаю полностью **на русском языке**. Следующий модуль — **Dynamic Organization & Program Formation Engine v0.1**: он использует реальные потоки спроса, ресурсов, совместной работы и bottleneck’ов, чтобы обнаруживать, где временная команда должна стать постоянной структурой, где несколько проектов логично объединить в программу, а где наоборот организацию следует разделить.

# Dynamic Organization & Program Formation Engine v0.1

## 157. Главный переход

До этого Universal Capability Market решал:

```text
Проекту нужна Capability X
↓
найти Resource
↓
создать Binding
↓
выполнить работу
```

Но со временем World State начинает видеть повторяющиеся структуры:

```text
одни и те же capabilities
+
одни и те же люди
+
одни и те же инструменты
+
одни и те же типы задач
+
одни и те же bottleneck'и
```

Возникает новый вопрос:

> Если комбинация ресурсов повторяется снова и снова, не должна ли она стать устойчивой организационной единицей?

---

# 158. Временная команда → постоянная структура

Например:

```text
Проект A:
Security Engineer
+
AI Security Agent
+
Threat Modeling Tool
```

Проект B требует практически тот же набор.

Проект C — снова.

Система обнаруживает:

```text
повторяющийся Capability Bundle
```

и создаёт гипотезу:

```text
Shared Security Office
```

---

# 159. Организация больше не статична

Классическая организационная структура обычно задаётся сверху:

```text
дирекция
↓
отдел
↓
группа
↓
сотрудник
```

Здесь появляется дополнительное направление:

```text
реальный поток работы
↓
повторяющиеся capability clusters
↓
организационная гипотеза
```

---

# 160. Это не означает автоматическое создание отделов

Очень важно различать:

```text
DETECTED PATTERN
```

и:

```text
ORGANIZATIONAL DECISION
```

AI может обнаружить:

```text
20 проектов регулярно требуют security review
```

Но решение:

```text
создать постоянный отдел безопасности
```

остаётся отдельным `DECISION`.

---

# 161. Основная формула

```text
Работа
↓
Повторяющиеся потребности
↓
Повторяющиеся Resource Bundles
↓
Организационный паттерн
↓
Организационная гипотеза
↓
Проверка
↓
Решение
↓
Организационная структура
```

---

# 162. Что такое Organizational Unit

Организационная единица может быть представлена как:

```text
RESOURCE type = TEAM / ORGANIZATION
```

Например:

```text
Security Office
Grant Office
Evaluation Lab
Data Team
Robotics Cell
```

Новый фундаментальный тип IIR не требуется.

---

# 163. Organizational Unit имеет Capability Portfolio

Например:

```text
Security Office
PROVIDES
threat_modeling

Security Office
PROVIDES
security_review

Security Office
PROVIDES
incident_response
```

То есть отдел определяется не только названием, а тем:

```text
что он умеет делать
```

---

# 164. Это принципиально отличается от оргсхемы

В обычной оргсхеме:

```text
Department X
```

может существовать просто потому, что он исторически создан.

В Capability Organization:

```text
Department X
```

имеет явную связь:

```text
Department X
PROVIDES
Capability Set
```

---

# 165. Demand-Driven Organization

Организационная структура может частично выводиться из:

```text
Demand Graph
```

Если capability:

```text
agent_evaluation
```

требуется:

```text
2 раза в год
```

постоянный отдел, вероятно, не нужен.

Если:

```text
80 проектов в год
```

ситуация другая.

---

# 166. Но частота — не единственный фактор

Нужно учитывать:

```text
частоту спроса
объём работы
критичность
специализацию
координационные издержки
scarcity
конфиденциальность
необходимость накопления знаний
```

---

# 167. Organizational Formation Vector

Вместо одного score:

```text
Repeated Demand
Shared Capabilities
Shared Resources
Knowledge Reuse
Coordination Frequency
Strategic Importance
Scarcity
Confidentiality
Operational Continuity
```

---

# 168. Пример: Grant Office

World State показывает:

```text
32 проекта
```

за год требовали:

```text
grant search
eligibility analysis
proposal writing
budget preparation
reporting
```

И каждый проект собирал эти capabilities заново.

Hypothesis:

```text
создать Shared Grant Office
```

---

# 169. Проверка гипотезы

Сравнить:

```text
Current:
project-by-project external consultants
```

и:

```text
Alternative:
shared internal Grant Office
```

По:

```text
стоимости
времени
knowledge retention
throughput
quality
```

---

# 170. Organization Formation — это тоже Project

Создание отдела нельзя считать мгновенным state change.

Это:

```text
Organization Formation Project
```

с задачами:

```text
определить capabilities
назначить руководителя
набрать команду
создать процессы
подключить инструменты
создать SLA
```

---

# 171. Organizational Unit может начинаться как Virtual Team

Полезная последовательность:

```text
ad-hoc team
↓
repeated team
↓
shared service
↓
formal organizational unit
```

Это позволяет не создавать bureaucracy слишком рано.

---

# 172. Team Persistence Detector

Система смотрит:

```text
одни и те же Resources
```

повторно появляются в проектах.

Например:

```text
Person A
Person B
AI Agent C
Tool D
```

встречаются совместно в 12 проектах.

Это:

```text
Persistent Collaboration Cluster
```

---

# 173. Но совместная встречаемость ≠ хорошая команда

Нужно различать:

```text
часто назначались вместе
```

и:

```text
успешно работали вместе
```

Второе требует Outcome Evidence.

---

# 174. Collaboration Evidence

Можно учитывать:

```text
task completion
handoff failures
review cycles
coordination delays
project outcomes
```

но не превращать это в скрытый социальный рейтинг людей.

---

# 175. Team Capability

Команда может обладать emergent capability, которой нет у одного человека.

Например:

```text
Researcher
+
Engineer
+
Product Specialist
```

вместе способны:

```text
translate research into product
```

Никто по отдельности полностью этого capability не предоставляет.

---

# 176. Emergent Team Capability

Это можно выразить:

```text
TEAM Resource
PROVIDES
research_to_product_translation
```

с Evidence из прошлых проектов.

---

# 177. Capability Bundle Detector

Система ищет наборы:

```text
A + B + C
```

которые часто требуются вместе.

Например:

```text
browser automation
agent evaluation
security
observability
```

---

# 178. Bundle становится Archetype

Можно создать:

```text
Agent Infrastructure Team Archetype
```

с:

```text
MUST:
agent systems
security

SHOULD:
evaluation
observability
```

---

# 179. Новый профессиональный Archetype

Повторяющийся capability bundle может указывать на формирование новой роли.

Например:

```text
browser automation
+
LLM agents
+
evaluation
+
sandboxing
```

может сформировать:

```text
Agent Runtime Engineer
```

Но это остаётся:

```text
Role Archetype Hypothesis
```

пока pattern недостаточно устойчив.

---

# 180. Role Emergence Detector

Он анализирует:

```text
job demand
talent profiles
project requirements
team structures
```

и ищет recurring capability combinations.

---

# 181. Очень важно не путать роль и capability

Например:

```text
Rust Engineer
```

— role label.

Но underlying capabilities:

```text
systems programming
memory safety
performance engineering
distributed systems
```

Именно capability layer остаётся canonical.

---

# 182. Organization Archetypes

Полезные типы organizational units:

```text
CAPABILITY TEAM
PLATFORM TEAM
SERVICE OFFICE
RESEARCH LAB
PROGRAM OFFICE
VALIDATION CENTER
SHARED INFRASTRUCTURE
```

---

# 183. Capability Team

Например:

```text
AI Security Team
```

обслуживает разные projects.

---

# 184. Platform Team

Создаёт:

```text
shared software platform
```

которую используют многие teams.

---

# 185. Service Office

Например:

```text
Grant Office
Legal/IP Office
Procurement Office
```

---

# 186. Research Lab

Создаёт и развивает scientific capability.

Например:

```text
Tactile Intelligence Lab
```

---

# 187. Program Office

Координирует:

```text
несколько связанных проектов
```

с общими milestones/resources.

---

# 188. Validation Center

Предоставляет:

```text
testing
benchmarking
certification
review
```

---

# 189. Shared Infrastructure

Например:

```text
GPU cluster
robotics lab
evaluation platform
```
